strengths: Synth-SBDH makes a useful clinical-NLP resource contribution suitable for Findings: 8,767 synthetic examples covering 14 SBDH categories and pain, with spans, assertion status, temporality, and rationales. Its intended unrestricted availability addresses a practical obstacle to clinical NLP research.

The central augmentation claim has substantive empirical support. Evaluation includes two real clinical datasets, multiple model architectures, classification and NER, and three independent runs. Improvements extend beyond the synthetic benchmark; for example, standard RoBERTa classification on VA-SBDH improves from 72.38 to 80.71 macro F.

Expert review of the entire 1,755-example synthetic test split is valuable. Two experienced annotators correct, discard, and add annotations through adjudication, and the paper transparently documents consequential errors, including confusion between prescribed medication and substance abuse.

The generation prompt, 45 seed examples, category definitions, filtering procedure, annotation guidelines, and training configurations provide substantial methodological documentation. Category-level results, training-size experiments, and an additional real-data pretraining comparison strengthen the evaluation.
weaknesses: The headline language overstates the consistency and breadth of improvements. Encoder NER gains are negligible or negative in some cases, and larger Llama models receive little benefit. The exceptionally large T5 improvement starts from an unstable baseline with 18.24-point standard deviation in macro F. The 94.44-point housing improvement is promising but rests on only 18 positive test examples; variation across training seeds does not establish uncertainty over the test population.

The experiments establish practical augmentation utility more clearly than the advantages of this particular synthesis design. There are no comparisons against class rebalancing or simpler augmentation, nor a target-data training control matched for the additional optimization budget. Appendix D.2 usefully matches pretraining steps, but its MIMIC comparison also differs in category coverage and label distribution, limiting attribution.

The claim of distilling reasoning capability is stronger than the evidence. DSS improves macro F by only 0.66 and 0.58 points on the synthetic test set, with the latter nonsignificant (P=0.36). Without rationale-content controls or evaluation of DSS transfer to real clinical text, these results demonstrate at most a small auxiliary-supervision benefit.

The expert-reviewed benchmark retains methodological limitations. Appendix E.2 explicitly permits retaining whichever plausible category GPT-4 selected while preferring a more specific category for newly added annotations, making labeling depend on the initial model output. The 71.06% alignment statistic also combines unchanged annotations with added omissions in its denominator; clearer per-attribute reliability and annotation precision/recall would better characterize quality.

Several advertised capabilities remain weakly validated. Experiments retain positive-presence annotations and do not directly evaluate temporality prediction or assertion-status classification. Synthetic examples average only 13.7 words, and real-data evaluation follows target-domain fine-tuning, so the evidence supports supervised transfer more directly than broad clinical generalizability.

Reporting needs reconciliation: the stated split sizes sum to 8,727 rather than 8,767, and Table 14 repeats several ClinicalMamba means and standard deviations from Table 3 for Llama 3.2. Downstream prompt templates and generation settings are insufficiently specified in the manuscript, while the private VA corpus limits independent replication. The approximately $90 cost comparison also omits expert seed creation and test-set review, so it does not establish the full cost advantage of the reviewed resource.
